items.expected_literal:
Author /workspace/solve.jq containing exactly one jq program:
  ["id","name","tags"], (.[] | [.id, .name, (.tags | join(";"))]) | @csv
The header row is emitted via a literal string array. Each input
record is projected to three columns where the tags array is
joined by ';' inside a single field and the whole row is passed
through @csv. @csv wraps every string in double quotes and
doubles any embedded double-quote octet, so embedded ",", '"',
';', and newline bytes in tag payloads survive the round trip
through csv.reader with a comma delimiter. The program is
portable across the public input and the private holdout by
construction because it does not embed any input-specific
literals.

items.expected_literal:
Another common wrong move is
  .[] | [.id, .name, .tags[]] | @csv
which explodes each record into one csv row per tag, breaking
the one-record-per-row invariant. The row count mismatch alone
fails D3, even before the tags-column-shape check runs.

items.expected_literal:
The classic wrong move is to write
  .[] | "\(.id),\(.name),\(.tags | join(";"))"
which concatenates csv bytes by hand. Any tag carrying an
embedded comma splits the row into extra columns, any tag
carrying an embedded double-quote octet breaks csv quoting,
and any tag carrying an embedded newline splits the row across
physical lines. csv.reader then either raises or produces a
row list that does not equal the expected list, and the D3
verifier check fires.
